summary:
The Aysén region stands under Chile's national framework. Gender Identity Law 21,120 has been in force since 27 December 2019 and allows adults to change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry, without therapy or surgery. Applicants aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and the statute provides no route for those under 14, although it recognises them as transgender. On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the "over 14 years old" wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl; that ruling applies only to the case before it.

Discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity has been prohibited since the 2012 Zamudio Law, which was extended to gender expression in 2018 and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates have offered a third sex option for intersex children since 2006.

No source in this inventory records a legal, incident or enforcement finding specific to Aysén. The Outright International Chile country dossier, published 12 March 2026, carries no Aysén-specific finding, so a visitor's expectations in the region rest on national law and national case data.

Recorded abuse against sexual and gender-diverse people is rising both nationally and in Aysén. Movilh's XXIV Annual Human Rights Report (HECHOS 2025, published March 2026) places the region at 0.65% of nationally documented abuse cases, a 25% year-on-year increase, and warns that this share reflects weaker local safety arrangements rather than low risk. Nationally the report counts 3,620 cases and complaints of discrimination in 2025, up 27.1% and the highest figure in 24 years. Only Valparaíso (-17.56%) and Metropolitana (-14.35%) recorded declines; the other 14 regions rose, which the report reads as hatred expanding into regions with less public debate.

Transphobic violence remains documented at national level. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime; the perpetrator, an acquaintance, confessed. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Detention carries specific guarantees. Gendarmería de Chile's national director signed a protocol covering the gender identity of trans detainees: placement by assumed gender, segmented housing, entry examinations, and a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

Care access is established but contested. The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. Circular 7 of June 2024 suggested deferring the start of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published; the Medical College noted that physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by seven votes to three, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents. In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program through the 2026 Budget Law, an action condemned by civil society groups and the national ombudsman for children; the Ministry of Health-run programme continues to provide support in medical centres, and the Crece con Orgullo programme has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. The Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Restrictive proposals are active but non-binding. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report, 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, a non-binding recommendation to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors and repeal the circular protecting gender identity in schools.
tangentialFactors:
The national pattern is one of expansion rather than concentration. Two regions, Valparaíso and Metropolitana, recorded declines of 17.56% and 14.35% respectively while the remaining 14 regions rose, which Movilh reads as documented hatred moving into regions where public debate over diverse sexual orientation and gender identity is weaker. Aysén's 0.65% share of national cases therefore sits within a broader shift of reporting away from the two largest urban regions, and its 25% year-on-year rise exceeds the national growth rate of 27.1% only in relative terms against a small base.

The defunding of the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program was condemned by civil society groups and the national ombudsman for children, and it sits alongside a non-binding Chamber of Deputies report approved on 15 May 2025 that recommends repealing the circular protecting gender identity in schools. Neither instrument alters the statute in force, but both signal parliamentary hostility toward the support architecture around minors.

outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records an Aysén-specific incident, arrest, court decision or enforcement action, and the Outright International Chile country dossier of 12 March 2026 contains no Aysén-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding. Whether the national protocol and circulars are applied as written by regional authorities is not sourced here.

Movilh's 2025 edition does not reproduce the region's 2024 share of documented cases, so the base for the reported 25% year-on-year rise cannot be verified from this inventory. The report's own caution that Aysén's 0.65% share reflects weaker local safety arrangements rather than low risk is an interpretation by the reporting organisation, not a measured regional risk rate.

The 9 April 2025 Constitutional Court ruling on the "over 14 years old" wording applies only to the case before it, and its effect on routine applications for younger children is not resolved by any source here. The CEI 57 report approved on 15 May 2025 is expressly non-binding; whether any of its recommendations has since been legislated is not sourced.
